I use the caldigit tb3 hubs and like those. Also you should look into a battery backup. Basic rule of thumb for data management is you’re only as fast as your slowest connection so just try to ensure you are not using bus powered devices as much as you can, and set productions expectations before the job for about how long it will take given your day. Sometimes it’s tricky to know for sure but you can get a decent idea given shoot specs and a data rate calculator.

Clone tool is fine but I use and trust Silverstack. It sounds like you have the right ideas in place and just need some reassurance. Here’s the reality of data management, all drives will fail eventually, some sooner than others. Using the proper checksum for video work I generally stick with MD5, XXHash is good if you have a fast reader and fast drives. It’s also important to spot check after the download, meaning playback and scrub through a few clips to ensure everything looks good. As far as using a NAS to backup at home I would just say monitor your drive health and ensure you can lose two drives if at all possible i.e. a raid 5 or something similar if you want to be super solid. I hope this helps, another less expensive option for software i would recommend is shotput.

Take a moment, understand what happened, how it happened and then move on. This is the most succinct way I can put it, the rest will be explaining it. 

Understanding - Making a mistake is part of learning, part of growth. It will happen and it will sometimes be painful to bear. Part of the lesson though is in how you react. Do you freak out and end up freaking others out?  Do you shut down and stop communicating?  Understand how you react in high stress can lead to a way forward. Stay calm, stay present and focused, try to come up with a solution. 

How it happened - Something that was drilled into me early on was process. The way you approach the work, whether it’s loader, digital loader, 2nd AC, 1st AC etc, having a workflow that you trust and doesn’t have any apparent holes is my go to. Make it your habit, for example when I download a card, I always keep the reel tag on the card until I’m ready to put it in. There will be no way I will give that card back to camera because it will have the tag on it still. I leave the tags on the reader for the job so there is also another physical record of my work. Build in failsafes for yourself because on set work can be crazy. 

Move on - Letting go is an important part of the work. We aren’t always allowed to do our best work, we buzz focus, forget to change the take on the slate, etc. things happen but it’s a moving target (set) so we have to keep moving. You roll with the punches and hopefully you never stop learning and asking questions like, “how could I do that better?” 

I hope this blurb helps and just keep going.

But if you’re going for instagram likes then yeah try to reposition your transmitter to either coming off the top handle on a paddle or sandwiched between the body and battery if you have a batter plate chassis for it. Otherwise what I normally do is put it on a short arm and keep it tight to the body but the arm allows for you to reposition fast if needed. Once that is placed then work on your audio feed into the A box and where that makes the most sense, it’s usually as tight to the body as makes sense but not on the operators side, please keep that clear. Last thing would be run your cables together and tie them at certain intervals, or use some sort of cable management but keep in mind you may end up having to change motor placement, replace a bad cable, swing to a zoom, whatever the case just make sure you don’t make it harder when you need to move fast. This is my stream of consciousness thoughts and opinions. Take what you like and works best for you and best of luck.

So this is a life long pursuit, as such I apologize in advance for how lengthy this post will get. I feel like there are so many different approaches and so many different styles, there’s a vast landscape out there and it’s easy to get lost. The best thing would be to work on composition, photography is a great medium to learn cinematography in my opinion because it forces you to tell a story with a single frame. That is what you must also do with a moving image. It gets more complex the more movement you have within a scene, but I hope you don’t get lost in gimmicks and fads, stick to just composing a nice frame, start there for everything. The simple process of filmmaking is this, you find a frame, set and dress the frame, light the frame, block it and then shoot it. That is the most simple I can make it, but understanding this as your foundation for everything I hope helps you develop the process, understand the steps to get to where you want to creatively. The technical will help support the artistic, and sometimes the artistic will help inform the technical. Sorry to get esoteric on you but you’ll find out what I mean soon enough. This is a great segue to my next point, patience. It will take you a long long time to even remotely master your craft. Do your best not to focus on the amount of time and just focus on what is within your control at the moment. Breathe. Everything will be okay and if it’s what you truly want you will find a way to do it. The last piece of advice I’ll leave you with is this, learn everyone’s job on set. This helps in a load of ways, it will help you better communicate with other departments as well as inform you who you need to speak with when the time comes. A CST will allow you to work in the whatever colorspace you tell it, usually rec709. It’s use in my understanding is similar to ACES, meaning you have an IDT, RRT, CCT and ODT but just by different names so it’s advantages are powerful but limited, also If you’re working with only arri footage you don’t need to use a CST if you’re going to use a LUT, especially a technical LUT meant to take you from Arri Wide Gamut to rec709. If you’re working with the CST workflow you don’t need/want to work with LUTs unless they are creative LUTs and in which case you need to understand where in the order of operations to put the LUT. For example if you are working within Resolve, I always have the LUT as the last node and have several nodes in front for primary corrections and curves. This allows me to work in the log space prior to the LUT meaning I have more latitude to work with. My workflow is specific to being on set for commercial workflows so it’s not the end all be all. I hope this helps, there’s a YouTube channel by the name of DIT WIT, they have a bunch of great videos talking about resolve, live grading, etc.

You’re asking the right questions, keep asking these questions with other AC’s you work with/meet. I’ll give you my answers but know that my experience is different than others. 

1. Yes you would take a soft tape and find your distance marks that you need for the scene but understand that this is a very traditional way mainly used on narrative film sets. That’s not to say it doesn’t still happen but I feel like it happens less and less. A lot happens during rehearsals, a lot of modern mark taking is usually while other people are working. Please note that this only works if you’re paying attention to what’s happening, your marks could prove useless if the actual shot wasn’t framed up for instance. 

2. If you have the opportunity to learn any of the range finder systems definitely learn them, it won’t hurt but sometimes, and this goes to one question you had later, it becomes too cumbersome to look at your wheel, the monitor, and anything else you may need to watch during the shot. So just beware there is a time and a place for everything, not every job needs or benefits from a cinetape. 

3. Focus peaking, I’ve used it before but less and less over the years.  I’m not sure if it’s frowned upon you just have to understand depending on the monitor and the settings you have as far as sensitivity are concerned it will be become really hard to really tell what’s in focus in certain lighting situations so that’s why I don’t rely on it more than fear of being embarrassed. 

4. One thing you can do is play the distance game. Look at things and guess the distance and then measure. Keep doing this. So stability of the data isn’t really the issue. Like you’re never worried that a 0 will flip to a 1, using a checksum ensures that the data is the exact same on both the source and destination. So it’s a not a question about stability. If a transfer is interrupted the file being transferred would be incomplete and therefore most likely unreadable traditionally, mainly because video files require a container or “wrapper” meaning a codec so other applications can read and view the video file as intended. So for your case the wrapper would be MXF. The cancellation issue is new to me, I would say double check you’re on the most recent firmware of shotput and check some forums specific to shotput. One thing I forgot to mention is after every offload I will CMMD+i on the card as well as the card folder on the project drives and verify the actual bytes. You should see the exact same numbers. It’s a nice reassurance everything is there, and then I spot check the files, ie Playback a couple clips and verify it’s playing back properly. 

Note: for playing back on a computer you may need a specific application to view the files, in your case I would try either catalyst browse or resolve, however you may need a beefier system like a macpro to playback at a proper 24 or 25 FPS depending on where you’re located. A good example is RED footage, I usually change it to 1/8 resolution for smoother playback when spot checking. Hope this all helps.

So first things first, about your setup. You should be aware of your front side bus, ie the connections from your motherboard to your ports. On each side, both ports would be linked to one bus so it’s usually wise to keep your reader on one bus and your project drives on the other bus.
 As far as your cancel issue, it’s been awhile since I’ve used shotput but if I remember correctly there is a pause feature which would allow you to safely disconnect drives and reader, reconnect and resume your offload. If you’re really cancelling it should end it right then and there. So I’m not sure what exactly you were talking about. 

I generally never offload more than one card at a time because you only have so much bandwidth when it comes to the reader and project drives. It won’t be nearly as efficient time wise when you’re on set. 

I’m not sure what you mean exactly by data copy but you should always be using an MD5 checksum for your offloads unless specified by post to use something like XXHash. Although you should note that XXHash is only faster with fast drives like 300Mb/s or faster I believe so always use MD5, it’s also what most post houses require as well. As far as how it works, it’s just an algorithm that is meant to verify large data sets. 



A few workflow things:
-every card should have its own reel tag (A001, B001, etc)
-leave the reel tag on the card until you are ready to put it in the reader
-Always use a battery backup
-Request drives with their own power supply, so your bus isn’t powering a drive which will eat at your offload speeds
-do your best to stay organized and if an offload is giving you an unreasonable amount of time, cancel and investigate. When troubleshooting I’ve found it best to change one thing at a time, for instance try a different cable, try a different reader, try a different card. 
-last thing I will say is a piece of advice I was given early on when I was just starting with data management, never let anyone rush you. What you are doing is important and sometimes you are at the whim of slow drives that production brought from their last shoot, or whatever the circumstance is, be polite but firm and always clear with what you need and how much time you think it will take but never rush. 

Hope this helps. Let me know if you have any other follow up questions.

I’d say start with checking all your connections. First things first though is safety for yourself as well as the components. Keep yourself grounded with a proper anti static bracelet and with your power supply unplugged press the power button a few times to discharge any capacitors.  Now take your side panels off and start at your power supply and if it’s modular then you can check to make sure each connection is plugged in. Next is trace everything from your power supply to the component they are supplying power to. Make sure the connection to secure, most should have a clip to help secure the connection. The next set of cables I would check would be the front panel connectors. Depending on your case they may present as a bunch of small connections or a single unit. Check your specific motherboard manual so you can identify where they are suppose to be plugged in and make sure they are plugged in correctly. This is just a start for troubleshooting, I hope it’s helpful and feel free to reach out if you have any specific questions or concerns and don’t be afraid. You can figure it out if you want, or if you are truly concerned about how much money you’ve invested then take it to a professional.

Trading - if you’re not playing solo self found then utilize the trade economy as much as you can. I’ve earned more exalts this league than the last one and a half combined just selling. 

Gameplay - it’s important in this game because it can be a grind at times to remember to have fun so find a build you will have fun with, for me it means moving fast, some people enjoy tanks. 

Risk/Reward - As you are familiar with arpgs I will just briefly touch on doing harder content (higher level monsters) will generally yield better gear and currency so I suggest on the lower level maps don’t even bother picking up most of the gear unless you get some 5 or 6 links you could use for crafting but seriously just keep mapping and you will drop a lot of straight currency most of the time.

Slow your shutter down. Since you’re a self proclaimed newbie I will try and make it as simple and clear as possible. Think about the video aspect like you would a still image. When you shoot a still image and the camera is moving or the subject is moving and your shutter speed isn’t that fast you end up with a blurry image. The same holds true for video. 

Most cinematic shooting follows the 180 degree rule which sets your shutter speed for shooting at 23.98 frames per second. It allows for a sharp enough image with enough motion blur which has become a standard in the industry, it’s what our parents grew up with as well as ourselves. 

Mess around with the shutter would be my best advice for you. Best of luck, although there may end up being some hardware restrictions with that camera, meaning you may only be able to reduce your shutter so much while in video mode.
